name: Apocryphal, Deuterocanonical & Pseudepigraphal Texts
description: Machine-readable index of the collection. Every text file is listed with its format, edition, translator, source and rights basis, so that a consumer need not guess any of them from the filename or sniff the layout.
readingOrder: The `phase` and `order` fields reproduce the reading order set out in README.md: phase 1 is the deuterocanonical core, phase 2 the pseudepigrapha and apocalyptic literature, phase 3 the New Testament apocrypha and Gnostic texts.

conventions.paths: All paths are relative to the repository root and use forward slashes. Directory and file names are not derivable from the book name; always use the paths given here.
conventions.primary: A file marked "primary": true is the recommended machine-readable edition of that text. Where a book has several primary files (Additions to Daniel) they are separate compositions, not alternative editions of one.
conventions.scripture: A file marked "scripture": false is not a translation of the ancient text and must not be served as one. See nonScripture below for the full list.
conventions.verseOrder: Every text file carries a verseOrder derived by reading the file. "monotonic": true means verse numbers ascend within each chapter. Where it is false, either outOfOrderChapters names the chapters that do not -- Charles transposed verses he judged displaced, and this collection follows his arrangement rather than renumbering it -- or "scope": "whole file" means the file has no chapter headings and its numbers do not form a single ascending run. Do not assume a monotonic sequence when iterating. Two further keys appear where a file needs them: "chapterOrder", present only when the chapters themselves do not run in ascending order, and "gaps", naming the chapters whose verse numbers skip. Neither affects the meaning of "monotonic", which is only ever about verse numbers inside a chapter.
conventions.rights: Every file carries a rights status and a basis. "public-domain" is asserted per file, never in bulk. Files whose basis could not be established carry status "unverified"; one file is "cc-by-nc-nd-4.0" and is NOT public domain. See NOTICE.md for the full record.
conventions.encoding: Every markdown file in the collection is UTF-8 with LF line endings; a .gitattributes file keeps them that way. Read them as UTF-8, without encoding detection, and the ^...$ anchored patterns below will match whether the file came from a checkout or over HTTP.
conventions.structure: Some file entries carry a `structure` object saying where the translation sits inside the file and how it is divided. For a sectioned-prose file that is `sectionHeading` (and, where the sections are numbered, `sectionNumber`, whose first capture group is the number). For a prose-with-apparatus file it is `sections`, one entry per part of the file, each marked "translation", "editorial" or "mixed", with `textStart` and `textEnd` naming the first and last line of the translated run inside a part that holds one. Anything not marked "translation" is the translator's own matter, or the chrome of the site the file was taken from, and must not be served as text.

chapter-caps-verse-lines.description: Chapter headings on their own line as `CHAPTER <n>`. Each verse is a single blank-line-separated line beginning `<n> ` (verse number, space, text).

chapter-title-verse-lines.description: As chapter-caps-verse-lines, but the chapter heading is title-cased: `Chapter <n>`.

chapter-caps-cv-lines.description: Chapter headings as `CHAPTER <n>`. Verses are consecutive (not blank-line-separated) lines beginning `<chapter>:<verse> `.

verse-lines.description: Single-chapter text with no chapter headings. Each verse is a blank-line-separated line beginning `<n> `.

gutenberg-douay-rheims.description: Project Gutenberg Douay-Rheims layout. Chapter headings are `<Book name> Chapter <n>`. Verses are blank-line-separated paragraphs opening `<chapter>:<verse>. ` and may wrap over several lines. Douay editorial footnotes appear between verses as ordinary paragraphs with no verse marker; a parser that assumes every paragraph is a verse will ingest them as scripture. Each file retains the Project Gutenberg header and footer, which are not part of the text.
caveats: Project Gutenberg header and footer present

cv-paragraphs.description: Chapter headings as `CHAPTER <n>` (optionally followed by a roman numeral in parentheses), with the translator's own section headings on their own lines above them. Verses are blank-line-separated paragraphs opening `<chapter>:<verse> `. A verse may carry continuation lines indented four spaces, which preserve the translator's line layout in poetic passages. A continuation line of the form `[<witness>: ...]` is apparatus -- a parallel recension in another language -- not part of the verse.
caveats: verses are not guaranteed to appear in numerical order; see verseOrder on each file

cv-paragraphs-ranged.description: As cv-paragraphs, but the roman numeral in the chapter heading is required rather than optional, and a verse marker may name a range (`<chapter>:<first>-<last>`) where the printed edition numbers two verses together. Used for a rendering derived from a prose-with-apparatus file whose printed chapter and verse numbers ran inside the prose and have been lifted out. The translation is delimited by bodyDelimiter. Verse numbers are the printed edition's: they may skip, and the chapters are not guaranteed to ascend. See verseOrder on each file.

numbered-paragraphs.description: No chapters. Sections or paragraphs are blank-line-separated and open `<n>. `.

paren-numbered-verses.description: Chapter headings as `CHAPTER <n>`; verses open `<n>) `. Verse numbers run continuously across the whole text rather than restarting at each chapter.

sectioned-prose.description: Named section headings on their own lines, followed by prose paragraphs. No verse numbers. Any bare numbers in the running text are manuscript page numbers, not verses. The translation is delimited by bodyDelimiter: the translator's front matter stands before the first such rule and the translator's notes after the second, and neither is part of the text. Headings are named rather than numbered, and the naming convention differs from one translation to the next, so each file entry carries its own sectionHeading pattern; where the sections are numbered it also carries sectionNumber, whose first capture group is that number. Match sectionHeading only inside the body: the translator's notes discuss sections by name and will otherwise match.
caveats: sectionHeading is declared per file, not here
a heading may wrap onto a second line; see the notes on each file

prose-with-apparatus.description: Continuous prose in which the translator's introduction, notes and the text itself are interleaved, with no consistent machine-readable structure. Suitable for reading and full-text search; not suitable for verse-level extraction without hand work. Where the parts of a file could be told apart by hand, its entry carries a `structure.sections` list naming each part and saying whether it is translation or the translator's own matter; where the text could be lifted out whole, the entry carries `derivedFile` naming a verse-addressable rendering of it in the same directory.

pdf.description: PDF. Some are digital typesetting with extractable text; some are image scans with none.

html.description: HTML page, including the source site's own markup and navigation.

rightsBasis.dedication: The translator or publisher has explicitly placed the work in the public domain.
rightsBasis.age-us-uk: Out of copyright by publication date in the United States and by author's death plus 70 years in the UK/EU.
rightsBasis.licensed: Under copyright, but distributed under a license that permits redistribution. Not public domain.
rightsBasis.unverified: No dedication found and no translator or date established. Treated as unresolved; see NOTICE.md.

books.name: 1 Enoch

files.edition: R. H. Charles, The Book of Enoch (S.P.C.K., 1917)
files.notes: All 108 chapters, 1,052 verses. Charles's editorial notation is preserved: [ ] editorial deletion, < > editorial addition, doubled brackets a reading restored from a secondary witness, dagger a corrupt reading. Where Charles printed a named witness in another language alongside the Ethiopic, the Ethiopic is the running text and the other witness follows as an indented `[Greek: ...]` or `[Latin Fragment: ...]` line, which is apparatus and not verse text. Where he printed an unnamed parallel column -- the doublets at 90:13-15 and 90:16-18 -- both belong to the chapter and both appear as ordinary verses. A small number of verse numbers that Charles set mid-clause are absorbed into the preceding verse. VERSES ARE NOT ALWAYS IN NUMERICAL ORDER: chapters 60, 90 and 106 follow Charles's transposed arrangement.

files.edition: M. R. James, The Apocryphal New Testament (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924)
files.notes: The three witnesses to the Apocalypse that James translates in full -- the Akhmim fragment, the Bodleian leaf and the Ethiopic text -- lifted out of the source file under the headings he gave them, with his introduction, his notes on each witness, his commentary and the scraped site chrome dropped. No word of the translation was changed. Two parts of the source are deliberately not in the body. The section headed `A.` is omitted outright: it interleaves six patristic quotations with James's own account of each one, inseparably, so serving it would serve his commentary as scripture. The Second Book of the Sibylline Oracles, which paraphrases the Apocalypse rather than being it, is kept after the closing body delimiter -- present for a reader, outside the text for a parser -- under a heading saying so. James's Akhmim verse numbers are left inline where he printed them; that fragment is separately verse-addressable in Apocalypse_of_Peter_Roberts-Donaldson.md.

Based on the Akhmim Greek fragment only, so much shorter than the James text. The file holds two independent numbered runs: the translated text, then a set of five patristic testimonia which restart at 1. Numbering is therefore not ascending across the file as a whole.
